sources.note: Decoded with topojson-client. The predecessor rattanakosin-kingdom feature has the same one-ring 199-position footprint within coordinate-transform noise and includes tested Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Nakhon Ratchasima and Pattani points.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1938 historical-basemap topology

It includes tested Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Nakhon Ratchasima and Pattani, but excludes Phuket and neighboring Lao, Cambodian and Burmese test points.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1945 historical-basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded with topojson-client. The successor thailand feature repeats the target footprint to within about 0.0014 degrees of transform noise. The 1945 change is an atlas id handoff rather than a meaningful national border reconstruction.

sources.title: Panarat Anamwathana, Thailand during World War II: Impact and Aftermath, Oxford DPhil thesis
sources.note: University of Oxford repository record and thesis checked for Thailand’s wartime political, economic and social history. The study emphasizes administrative continuity, severe economic contraction, inflation and shortages, the Japanese alliance, Free Thai resistance and a negotiated postwar transition rather than state collapse.

sources.title: Charnvit Kasetsiri, The First Phibun Government and Its Involvement in World War II
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Journal of the Siam Society study checked for Phibun’s rise, authoritarian government, nationalism, the 1939 name change, cultural mandates, relations with Japan, the July 1944 political defeat and the survival of the constitutional state.

sources.title: E. Bruce Reynolds, Thailand and Japan’s Southern Advance, University of California Press chapter
sources.note: University of California Press chapter checked for Thailand’s domestic politics and diplomacy before the Japanese invasion, including Phibun’s military government, nationalist state-building and the pressures created by war in Europe and Japanese expansion.

sources.title: Kobkua Suwannathat-Pian, National Identity, the “Sam-Sams” of Satun, and the Thai Malay Muslims
sources.note: Kyoto University Southeast Asian Studies article checked for Phibun-era nation-making and the unequal pressure placed on Malay Muslim communities by centralized language, dress, naming and cultural policies.

sources.title: Fine Arts Department of Thailand, collected state cultural mandates and documents
sources.note: Official Fine Arts Department document collection checked for the first 1939 cultural mandate. It preserves the Thai wording “ชื่อประเทศ ประชาชน และสัญชาติ ให้ใช้ว่า ‘ไทย’” ordering use of Thai for the country, people and nationality.

sources.title: UNESCO Memory of the World nomination, Minute Books of the Council of the Siam Society
sources.note: UNESCO nomination dossier checked for the Siam Society’s scholarly continuity, its meetings, publications, collections and the effect of wartime disruption. This is evidence about one learned institution, not the education of the whole population.

sources.title: Kenjiro Ichikawa, Thai Society During World War II
sources.note: Academic article checked for wartime Thai social and political responses, the Chinese anti-Japanese boycott, accommodation and compromise under Japanese military pressure, and the distinction between alliance and direct Japanese colonial administration.

sources.title: Public Relations Department, Battle of Ko Chang and the Franco-Thai War
sources.note: Thai government historical article checked for the 1940-1941 border dispute, nationalist demonstrations, land, air and naval fighting and the Battle of Ko Chang. The official commemorative viewpoint is used with attribution rather than as a neutral account of every combatant’s experience.

sources.title: U.S. Department of State, Foreign Relations of the United States, Japanese invasion of Thailand, 8 December 1941
sources.note: Primary diplomatic record checked for reports of Japanese landings and fighting on 8 December 1941, the Thai cease-fire and permission for Japanese forces to pass through the country. It records contemporary diplomatic information, not every local encounter.

sources.title: Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs, The Quest for a Thai-U.S. Alliance
sources.note: Official diplomatic history checked for the December 1941 Thai-Japanese alliance, Thailand’s January 1942 declarations of war, Ambassador Seni Pramoj’s refusal to deliver the declaration in Washington and the roots of the Free Thai relationship with the United States.

sources.title: U.S. Department of State, FRUS memorandum on Thailand’s declaration of war, 1942
sources.note: Primary U.S. diplomatic memorandum checked for the American decision not to declare war on Thailand after Ambassador Seni Pramoj withheld the Thai declaration. It documents U.S. policy; Britain and other Allies made different legal choices.

sources.title: U.S. Department of State, FRUS, Thai declaration ending war status, 1945
sources.note: Primary diplomatic document checked for Thailand’s August 1945 repudiation of the 1942 war declarations and wartime acts, and for the claim that those acts had been contrary to the Thai people’s will. It is a postwar government position, not a poll of every citizen.

sources.title: U.S. Department of State, FRUS, postwar settlement with Thailand, 1945
sources.note: Primary diplomatic record checked for competing Allied positions on Thailand after Japan’s surrender, including U.S. support for Thai sovereignty and British demands. It shows negotiation and continuity rather than an automatic return to the prewar situation.

sources.title: NIDA Library, Free Thai Movement Collection
sources.note: National Institute of Development Administration special-collection guide checked for Free Thai networks, participants, memoirs and archival materials. The collection supports the movement’s institutional breadth while also warning that surviving elite records do not capture every resister.

sources.title: Pridi Banomyong Institute, the Free Thai Movement and the end of World War II
sources.note: Institute historical essay checked for Regent Pridi Banomyong’s role, domestic Free Thai organization, contact with Allied forces and the August 1945 peace proclamation. It represents an institution devoted to Pridi’s legacy and is read with that perspective explicit.

sources.title: Gregg Huff and Shinobu Majima, Financing Japan’s Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere in Thailand
sources.note: Peer-reviewed economic history checked for forced occupation finance, monetary expansion, prices rising more than sevenfold from 1941 to 1945, Bangkok-Thonburi ration coupons from 1943, black markets and the especially heavy burden on urban households.

sources.title: Paul H. Kratoska, Food and Living Standards in Urban Southeast Asia during World War II
sources.note: Cambridge University Press chapter checked for wartime Bangkok shortages, rationing, urban displacement, Allied raids, mass evacuation and the April 1945 destruction of power stations. Its city evidence is not generalized to every rural household.

sources.title: Kakizaki Ichiro, Rail Transport and Rice Distribution in Thailand during World War II
sources.note: Kyoto University Southeast Asian Studies article checked for rail requisition, military transport, disrupted civilian movement and rice distribution during the war. It explains why a rice-exporting country could still face serious local shortages and high prices.

sources.title: Ubon Jirasawat, Political, Economic and Social Conditions of Thailand during World War II
sources.note: Chulalongkorn University thesis record checked for wartime administration, diplomacy, economic disruption and government attempts to prescribe a modern way of life. It is an older study and explicitly describes its evidence as incomplete and tentative.

sources.title: Australian War Memorial, Burma-Thailand Railway
sources.note: Australian War Memorial exhibition checked for the railway’s construction, approximately 60,000 Allied prisoners of war, about 200,000 Asian laborers, brutal work, disease, malnutrition and enormous death toll. Allied POW documentation is fuller than evidence for diverse Asian romusha.

sources.title: Australian War Memorial, Jonathon Dallimore: F Force on the Burma-Thailand Railway
sources.note: Australian War Memorial article checked for F Force’s 1943 forced movement, remote camps, cholera, inadequate food, medical scarcity and very high mortality. It is a focused prisoner-of-war case and does not stand for all railway workers.

sources.title: Chulalongkorn University, Thai women and state policy in the Phibun era
sources.note: Chulalongkorn University thesis record checked for government ideals of women as modern wives, mothers and citizens alongside women’s growing public visibility, schooling and employment. Prescriptive policy is distinguished from what every household actually did.

sources.title: Chulalongkorn University, family politics and nation-building under Phibun
sources.note: Chulalongkorn University thesis record checked for state efforts to make orderly marriage, gender roles, child-rearing and household conduct serve nation-building. Official family ideals are treated as campaigns, not a census of private life.

sources.title: Southeast Asian Studies, Women, Fashion, and Nation in Phibun-era Thailand
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Kyoto University journal issue checked for dress mandates, hats, skirts, blouses, urban fashion, women’s bodies as symbols of civilization and the uneven, negotiated reception of official clothing rules.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Malay Muslims and the Thai-Buddhist State
sources.note: Scholarly book chapter checked for the long relationship between Malay Muslim communities and the central Thai state, including language, Islamic education, local authority and twentieth-century assimilation pressure. The southern borderlands were not culturally uniform.

sources.title: Journal of Language and Culture, Chinese schools in Thailand before and during World War II
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Thai journal article checked for Chinese-language schooling, nationalist politics, state surveillance and wartime restrictions. It supports discussion of a substantial but politically pressured educational world, not a claim that all Chinese Thai children attended such schools.

sources.title: A boys’ school, militarized youth and health in Phibun-era Thailand
sources.note: Open-access scholarly article checked for school discipline, bodily training, uniforms, hygiene and the Yuwachon military youth movement. Its institutional case is vivid but cannot represent every rural school or every child.

sources.title: UNESCO, Education for All assessment: Thailand historical background
sources.note: UNESCO education assessment checked for the development of compulsory primary education, uneven school access and the long expansion of Thailand’s education system. Later aggregate data are used only as retrospective institutional context.

sources.title: Parliament Museum of Thailand, Democracy Monument
sources.note: Official Parliament Museum page checked for the Democracy Monument’s construction and inauguration in 1939-1940, its constitutional symbolism and its relationship to the new political order. Official symbolism is distinguished from public consent.

sources.title: Silpakorn University, history
sources.note: Official university history checked for the School of Fine Arts, Silpa Bhirasri’s role and the institution’s elevation to Silpakorn University in 1943. Founding an arts university during war was an enduring institutional achievement, though access was limited.

sources.title: The Demographic History of Thailand, public health and mortality
sources.note: Peer-reviewed demographic study checked for mortality, epidemics, vaccination and the interwar Sanitary Campaign, including field units, provincial expansion and thousands of latrines. National programs did not reach all communities equally.

sources.title: Of Germs, Public Hygiene, and the Healthy Body: The Making of the Medicalizing State in Thailand
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Journal of Asian Studies article checked for health education, hygiene, sanitation and state campaigns that linked clean bodies and surroundings with modern citizenship. It analyzes government power as well as health benefits.

sources.title: Historical development of sanitation and latrines in Thailand
sources.note: Scholarly sanitation history checked for household and public latrine development, rural sanitation campaigns, administrative law and the creation of the Ministry of Public Health in 1942. The evidence supports unequal transition, not universal flush toilets.

sources.title: Central Thai food culture and everyday meals
sources.note: Scholarly cultural study checked for rice-centered meals, shared dishes, fish, vegetables, condiments and the social organization of central Thai food. Retrospective cultural evidence is used cautiously and is not treated as a wartime ration diary.

Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

proposedOverrides.summary: An epic sourced 1938-1945 history of wartime Thailand: naming, war, resistance, family life, food, schools, medicine, toilets and Thai writing.

batchIdentityNotes: Targeted only exact id siam-1938: name Siam, approximately 1938-1945, kind state, datesApproximate true, and missing a card before integration.
The target has exactly one observed interval, 1938-1945, in world-1938.json; no features occur outside the indexed lifetime.
The exact feature is a one-ring Polygon with 199 coordinate positions and bounds approximately 97.37197,5.53111 to 105.47565,20.45810.
Point tests put Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Nakhon Ratchasima and Pattani inside; Phuket, Vientiane, Luang Prabang, Phnom Penh, Siem Reap, Yangon and Kuala Lumpur are outside.
Phuket’s exclusion is treated as an imported coastal geometry defect, not a historical secession. The card never makes political claims from that glitch.

The predecessor rattanakosin-kingdom and successor thailand outlines are equivalent to the target after allowing coordinate-transform noise; the successor maximum matched-position delta is approximately 0.0013543 degrees.
The separate id siam, 1800-1815, is a tiny three-part, 18-position imported feature that excludes all major tested Thai points. It is not associated with this card and receives no appliesTo entry.

The official country name changed from Siam to Thailand in 1939, back to Siam in English in 1945 and to Thailand again in 1949. The atlas label siam-1938 is therefore explicitly presented as a data label, not a clean historical state name.
The 1945 endpoint is treated as a dataset handoff and wartime political transformation, not collapse, conquest or a new country’s birth. No additional override is proposed.
